notes.meaning: After years of peace, the people of Israel turned away from God and fell back into idol worship. Because of their rebellion, God allowed the nation of Midian to conquer and rule over them for seven years. This hardship was meant to wake them up and turn their hearts back to Him.

The Midianites ruled with such cruelty that the Israelites fled from their own towns and farms. They hid in mountain ravines, caves, and rocky strongholds to protect their lives and whatever goods they could carry. Sin had taken away their courage, leaving them to live like fugitives in their own homeland.

Whenever the Israelites planted their crops, huge bands of Midianites, Amalekites, and other eastern nomadic tribes invaded the land. They brought their herds, tents, and countless camels, swarming across the countryside like a plague of locusts. These raiders destroyed the fields all the way to Gaza and took all the sheep, cattle, and donkeys, leaving the people with nothing to eat.

Israel was stripped of its food and wealth until the people were completely helpless. When their idols could not save them, they finally cried out to the Lord for rescue. God often allows people to reach the end of their own strength so they will look to Him.

When the people begged for help, God first sent an unnamed prophet to explain why they were suffering. The prophet reminded them how God had freed their ancestors from slavery in Egypt and given them this fertile land. God had commanded them never to fear or worship the local gods, but they had refused to listen to His voice.

The angel of the Lord came in the appearance of a traveler and sat beneath a great oak tree in the village of Ophrah. Nearby, a man named Gideon was beating out wheat with a stick inside a sunken winepress. He was working in secret so the Midianite raiders would not see the grain and steal it.

The heavenly visitor appeared to Gideon and greeted him as a brave and mighty warrior, promising that the Lord was with him. At that moment Gideon was hiding in fear, but God spoke to what he would become by divine power. God sees and calls out the strength He plans to give His servants.

Gideon asked how the Lord could truly be with Israel when the nation was suffering so terribly under Midian. He wondered why the great miracles done in Egypt were no longer happening, feeling that God had completely abandoned them. He did not yet realize that Israel's own disobedience had brought this disaster upon them.

The Lord looked straight at Gideon and commanded him to go and rescue Israel from the Midianites. God told him to go in the strength he had just received, backed by the promise that the Lord Himself was sending him. A divine calling supplies all the power needed to accomplish the task.

Gideon objected out of deep humility and fear, pointing out that his clan was the poorest in the tribe of Manasseh. He also considered himself the least important person in his father's household. He could not imagine how someone so lowly could ever lead a national deliverance.

The Lord answered Gideon's doubts with a firm promise: He would be right beside him in battle. Because God was with him, Gideon would defeat the entire Midianite army as easily as if fighting a single man. Victory does not depend on human numbers, but on God's presence.

Gideon asked for a miraculous sign to prove that this messenger was truly speaking for God. He begged the visitor to wait under the tree while he went to prepare food and bring it back as a gift. The Lord graciously agreed to stay until Gideon returned.

Gideon hurried inside and prepared a generous meal from a young goat and a large amount of flour baked into flat bread. He placed the meat in a basket, poured the broth into a pot, and brought everything out to the visitor under the oak tree. Even in a time of severe food shortages, he gave his guest the very best he had.

The angel told Gideon to place the meat and bread on a rock and pour the broth over them like a drink offering. When the angel touched the food with the tip of his staff, fire burst out of the rock and consumed the entire meal, and the angel vanished into thin air. This miracle showed that the visitor was no mere traveler, but God accepting an offering.

Gideon was struck with terror when he realized he had been talking face to face with the angel of the Lord. In ancient Israel, people believed that anyone who saw the holy God or His direct presence would die on the spot. His natural fear shows how sinful humans tremble before God's absolute holiness.

The Lord spoke directly to Gideon, speaking peace to his heart and telling him not to fear. God promised him that he was safe and would not die from this encounter. When God calls His people to serve Him, He calms their deepest fears.

In grateful response, Gideon built a stone altar in Ophrah to commemorate God's mercy and called it 'The Lord Is Peace.' This monument remained standing for many years as a reminder of God's gentle reassurance. Real peace with God gives believers courage to face dangerous duties.

That same night, God commanded Gideon to tear down his father's altar to the false god Baal and chop down the wooden Asherah pole next to it. Gideon was then told to build a proper altar to the Lord on top of the local stronghold and sacrifice a seven-year-old bull, using the pagan wood for fuel. Before Gideon could save the nation, he had to cleanse his own home of idolatry.

Gideon gathered ten trusted servants and obeyed everything God had commanded. Because he was afraid of being stopped or attacked by his family and the townspeople, he completed the work during the night. His faith was still young and fearful, but he chose to obey anyway.

The next morning, the men of the town woke up to find Baal's altar destroyed, the sacred pole chopped down, and a bull burning on a new altar to the Lord. After asking around and investigating, they discovered that Gideon had done it. Their prompt discovery forced the community to confront the truth about their idols.

The angry men confronted Gideon's father, Joash, and demanded that he bring out his son to be executed. They were furious that Baal's shrine had been destroyed, showing how deeply idolatry had taken hold of God's covenant people. They were willing to kill an Israelite to defend a helpless pagan idol.

Joash stood up to the angry crowd, arguing that if Baal were really a living god, he could easily defend himself against anyone who knocked down his altar. Anyone who tried to take Baal's place by executing Gideon would be the one put to death. From that day on, Gideon was called Jerubbaal, meaning 'let Baal contend,' because the idol had proven powerless to harm him.

The allied armies of Midian, Amalek, and other eastern desert tribes gathered, crossed the Jordan River, and set up camp in the wide Valley of Jezreel. They arrived during the harvest season expecting to plunder the land as they had done for years. God was drawing these enemies together for their final defeat.

The Spirit of the Lord came upon Gideon, clothing him with supernatural boldness and leadership. He blew a ram's horn trumpet to rally his own clan, and messengers went out through the northern tribes of Manasseh, Asher, Zebulun, and Naphtali. Thousands of men answered the call and marched out to join him in battle.

Facing a massive enemy army, Gideon asked God for a miraculous sign to confirm the promise of victory. He proposed placing a piece of wool on an open threshing floor overnight. If morning came with dew only on the wool while the surrounding dirt remained completely dry, he would know God was truly with him.

God granted the sign exactly as Gideon had asked. Early the next morning, Gideon picked up the fleece and wrung out a whole bowl full of water, even though the ground around it was dry. God showed great patience by meeting Gideon in his hesitation.

Knowing wool naturally holds moisture, Gideon humbly asked God not to be angry and requested one final test. This time he asked for the fleece to stay completely dry while the ground all around was soaked with dew. That night God did just that, leaving no doubt that His miraculous power was guiding Gideon.
